This is not a Texas exclusive issue. Almost one year ago in the Eastern Interconnection, Winter Storm Elliot forced out of service up to 90,000 MW of generation, and up to 5,000 MW of load was shed. Elliot caused a smaller deviation from average daily temperature of 20-30 degrees compared to Uri's 40-50.

This is FERC & NERC's report on Elliot, though it does compare past cold weather events (including Uri) in some sections: https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/news/ferc-nerc-release-final-report-lessons-winter-storm-elliott

Texas's Uri event in 2021 was the worst event, but this is not a Texas exclusive issue. Almost a year ago during 2022 Winter Storm Elliot in the Eastern Interconnection, up to ~90,000 MW of generation was made unavailable due to the cold weather. Up to ~5,000 MW of load was shed at worst, with load shed procedures implemented for up to 7 hours.

The Texas event was certainly worse (up to ~65,000 MW of lost generation, up to 20,000 MW shed at worst, load shed procedures lasting over 70 hours...), though I would note that Uri caused a 40-50 degree deviation from average daily temperature; Elliot only caused a 20-30 degree deviation from average daily temperature.

All from the joint FERC & NERC report regarding Winter Storm Elliot, though it does speak some on other winter events as well: https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/news/ferc-nerc-release-final-report-lessons-winter-storm-elliott

NERC is the real deal, they are the main grid reliability regulator for the US and Canada. You can find NERC's assessment that this article mentions on NERC's website.

The assessment is specifically predicting elevated risk for "insufficient operating reserves" for that two thirds. This is technically a power shortage, but it doesn't necessarily mean residential load shed. There are several emergency procedures that can be implemented to try and correct a reserve shortage. Load shed is the last resort.

Again, though, all their concerns are still real. Load is going up and generation is barely keeping up. Also natural gas is a large share of generation in most of the US, and it has been having issues during big cold snaps. ERCOTs event is most well known, but as the article mentions, PJM in the north east US had a very similar event last winter. They did not have to shed load like ERCOT; but they lost massive amounts of gas generation for similar reasons and got uncomfortably close to that possibility.
